turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels,
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and the two measured objectives `yield
    strength (MPa)` and `toughness (J)` (both at room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose
    objectives were NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same
    process/composition columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH toughness (J). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), toughness (J)) plane, so a set of mutually
non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates that are
all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**Structure of the data.** The 300 training steels fall into clear alloy families, and within each family the heat‑treat/aging temperature moves the point along a strong strength–toughness anti‑correlation:

| family (signature) | behaviour in train |
|---|---|
| Cr‑Mo‑V tempered martensitic (≈83–86 Fe, 11–13 Cr, low Ni) | temper/AH‑2 temp 300–450 °C → **1330–1450 MPa, 19–70 J**; 550–700 °C → 890–1090 MPa, 88–105 J |
| Ti‑hardened Fe‑Ni‑Cr superalloy‑type (11 Cr, 19–23 Ni, Ti≈2.9) | AH 700–750 °C → **700–1000 MPa with 72–114 J** (best "both" region) |
| 12Cr‑8.5Ni‑Ti‑Cu maraging PH | aging 400–450 °C → 1300–1600 MPa but 27–38 J |
| austenitic 18Cr–12Ni / 23Cr–13–18Ni | only 230–380 MPa but **200–370 J** |
| 23.5Cr–27Ni–Cu (Fe≈41) | 270 MPa / **350 J** (toughness champion) |

So a good frontier‑spanning set takes one point from each of several families, choosing the tempering/aging condition that keeps it non‑dominated.

**Picks and predicted objectives (by nearest‑neighbour interpolation on the identical compositions in train):**

- **c041** – 11.25Cr‑1.65Ni‑V martensitic, AH 450 °C: bracketed by 400 °C→1340 MPa/61 J and 550 °C→1090 MPa/88 J ⇒ **≈1280 MPa, ≈70 J** (strength anchor).
- **c044** – 11.25Cr‑23Ni‑2.9Ti, HT 1120 °C + AH 735 °C/16 h: sibling with 720/640 °C aging gave 1000 MPa/100 J ⇒ **≈950 MPa, ≈100 J**.
- **c008** – 11.25Cr‑19.5Ni‑2.9Ti, HT 1175 °C + AH 750 °C/16 h: siblings 710 MPa/114 J and 700 MPa/72 J ⇒ **≈720 MPa, ≈115 J**.
- **c025** – 23.5Cr‑13.5Ni austenitic, solution 1050 °C only: siblings 360 MPa/206 J and 280 MPa/300 J ⇒ **≈330 MPa, ≈230 J**.
- **c010** – 23.5Cr‑27Ni‑3Cu, solution 1050 °C/4.6 h, no aging: nearest twin gave 270 MPa/**350 J** ⇒ toughness anchor.

These five are mutually non‑dominated and stretch from ~1300 MPa (low J) to ~350 J (low MPa), with two well‑placed knee points (~950/100 and ~720/115) that come from the family that historically gives the best simultaneous strength–toughness.

Final: c041, c044, c008, c025, c010
